Bakbukiah
bak-bu-KYE-ah
n. (proper, a Levite of the restoration; Hebrew, the wasting of the LORD)
Hebrew Baqbuqyah, from baqbuq, a flask or bottle — a word formed from the gurgling sound a narrow-necked vessel makes. The name is usually read as emptied by Jehovah, or the wasting of the LORD.

Biblical Definition

He appears three times, always in a company and always with an office. At the settling of Jerusalem: “And Mattaniah the son of Micha, the son of Zabdi, the son of Asaph, was the principal to begin the thanksgiving in prayer: and Bakbukiah the second among his brethren” (Nehemiah 11:17). Among the singers set in order: “Also Bakbukiah and Unni, their brethren, were over against them in the watches” (Nehemiah 12:9) — antiphonal choirs, answering each other. And among the gatekeepers: “Mattaniah, and Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Meshullam, Talmon, Akkub, were porters keeping the ward at the thresholds of the gates” (Nehemiah 12:25). He is named as the second, never the principal. The restoration ran on men who held the second place, answered the other choir, and kept a door — and the Holy Ghost saw fit to write their names down.

Origin & Era

Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a Levite of the restoration, second among his brethren in the thanksgiving and a porter at the gates.

expand to see more

PORTER, n. A man that has the charge of a door or gate; a doorkeeper.

WARD, n. Watch; act of guarding; garrison; the state of being under guard or in custody.

ANTIPHONAL, a. Consisting of responsive singing; sung alternately by two choirs or divisions.

THANKSGIVING, n. The act of rendering thanks or expressing gratitude for favors or mercies.

SUBORDINATE, a. Inferior in order, in nature, in dignity, in power or importance; occupying a lower place.

Key Scripture

Nehemiah 11:17 — "And Mattaniah the son of Micha, the son of Zabdi, the son of Asaph, was the principal to begin the thanksgiving in prayer: and Bakbukiah the second among his brethren, and Abda the son of Shammua, the son of Galal, the son of Jeduthun."

Nehemiah 12:9 — "Also Bakbukiah and Unni, their brethren, were over against them in the watches."

Nehemiah 12:25 — "Mattaniah, and Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Meshullam, Talmon, Akkub, were porters keeping the ward at the thresholds of the gates."

Psalm 84:10 — "For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness."

Modern Corruption

Christian service is evaluated by prominence, so that a man in the second place is assumed to be waiting for the first; Scripture records Bakbukiah as the second, in a watch and at a gate, and preserves his name.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live distortion is a settled assumption that visibility measures value, which turns every subordinate office into a stepping stone and every long-held second place into a failure. Nehemiah 11:17 describes a man whose whole recorded identity is the second among his brethren. Nehemiah 12:9 has him in a watch, singing over against the other choir. Nehemiah 12:25 has him keeping the ward at a threshold. Three verses, three offices, none of them the first, and his name in the word of God in all three.

The psalmist of the sons of Korah — a family of doorkeepers — put the doctrine in a line: For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness. The comparison is not between a great office and a small one but between the meanest place in God's house and the best seat anywhere else. A man who has genuinely made that comparison stops calculating his position, and the church that is full of such men is the one that gets rebuilt.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Baqbuqyah (H1229), the wasting of the LORD; baqbuq (H1228), a flask; mishmar (H4929), a watch or ward; shower (H7778), a porter.

expand to see more

Hebrew Baqbuqyah (H1229) — Bakbukiah; emptied or wasted by Jehovah.

Hebrew baqbuq (H1228) — a bottle or flask, named for the sound it makes when poured.

Hebrew mishmar (H4929) — a watch, a guard; the courses the singers kept.

Hebrew shower (H7778) — a gatekeeper, a porter; his office in Nehemiah 12:25.

Hebrew towdah (H8426) — thanksgiving; what Mattaniah was principal to begin.

Usage

"“Bakbukiah the second among his brethren” — and named for it."

"“Were over against them in the watches” — choir answering choir."

"“I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God”."
